summary:
Project Summary – Planetary Analog

Planetary Analog explores Saudi Arabia’s volcanic landscapes as potential terrestrial analog environments for studying the Moon and Mars. The project focuses on Harrat Khaybar as the primary site for quantitative terrain analysis using NASA ASTER GDEM V003 data and GIS tools, while Harrat Rahat is included for descriptive geological comparison. Additional environmental data, including MERRA-2 dust measurements and land surface temperature layers, support the preliminary assessment. The project aims to identify geological and topographical similarities and differences that may contribute to future planetary research and space exploration. Quantitative comparisons with lunar and Martian datasets remain as future work.
details: Project Details – Planetary Analog Planetary Analog explores the potential of Saudi Arabia’s volcanic landscapes as terrestrial analog environments for studying selected geological and topographical characteristics of the Moon and Mars. Our project focuses on two volcanic regions: Harrat Khaybar and Harrat Rahat. Harrat Khaybar is the primary site for quantitative terrain analysis, while Harrat Rahat is included in a descriptive geological comparison. For Harrat Khaybar, we used NASA ASTER GDEM V003 elevation data, with an approximate spatial resolution of 30 meters. We processed the data using QGIS, GRASS GIS, and GDAL. Our workflow included defining the study area, clipping and reprojecting the DEM, and generating elevation, slope, aspect, and hillshade layers to examine the terrain. We also incorporated environmental datasets. NASA MERRA-2 aerosol data was used to examine regional atmospheric dust conditions, while land surface temperature layers were prepared for both study regions. The dust data has a relatively coarse spatial resolution, so its results are treated as regional estimates rather than detailed local measurements. The project’s creative approach is to combine geological information, terrain analysis, and environmental data to establish a preliminary framework for identifying potentially relevant terrestrial analog sites. Lunar and Martian datasets have also been identified for future comparative analysis; however, direct quantitative comparisons are still pending. We used NASA Earth observation resources and open-source GIS software, including QGIS, GRASS GIS, and GDAL. AI tools were used for limited assistance with research organization, writing, and language refinement, while the project workflow and analysis were carried out using the selected scientific datasets and GIS tools. The intended impact is to support planetary science education and preliminary research by demonstrating how Earth-based volcanic environments can help researchers investigate geological and terrain characteristics relevant to planetary exploration. The project is designed as an initial research framework, not as a final site-selection or landing-site recommendation.
